'''Vera Florence Cooper Rubin''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|r|uː|b|ɪ|n}}; July 23, 1928 – December 25, 2016) was an American [[astronomer]] who pioneered work on [[Galaxy rotation curve|galaxy rotation rates]].<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227">{{cite journal |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |author-link=Dennis Overbye |date=December 27, 2016 |title=Vera Rubin, 88, Dies; Opened Doors in Astronomy, and for Women |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/27/science/vera-rubin-astronomist-who-made-the-case-for-dark-matter-dies-at-88.html |journal=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=December 27, 2016}}</ref><ref name="VOX-20210817">{{cite news |last1=Pinkerton |first1=Byrd |last2=Hassenfeld |first2=Noam |date=August 17, 2021 |title=Astronomers were skeptical about dark matter – until Vera Rubin came along: She built a bullet-proof case for exploring the concept |url=https://www.vox.com/22576927/vera-rubin-dark-matter-astronomy-biography |access-date=August 17, 2021 |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> She uncovered the discrepancy between the predicted and observed [[angular motion]] of galaxies by studying [[Galaxy rotation curve|galactic rotation curves]], the first evidence for the [[galaxy rotation problem]], one key piece of evidence for [[dark matter]]. Measurements by other astronomers using 21 centimeter [[Hydrogen line| hydrogen line]] radio telescopes clinched the case.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=de Swart|first1=Jaco|last2=Bertone|first2=Gianfranco|last3=van Dongen|first3=Jeroen|date=2017|title=How dark matter came to matter|journal=Nature Astronomy|volume=1|issue=59|page=0059|arxiv=1703.00013|bibcode=2017NatAs...1E..59D|doi=10.1038/s41550-017-0059|s2cid=119092226}}</ref>

Honored during her lifetime for her work, she received the [[Bruce Medal]], the Gold Medal of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]], and the National Medal of Science, among others.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /> The [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]] in [[Chile]] is named in her honor.<ref name="Falk-2025">{{Cite web |last=Falk |first=Dan |title=This Revolutionary New Observatory Will Locate Threatening Asteroids and Millions of Galaxies: Beginning next year, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory will use the world's largest digital camera to give us a whole new view of the universe |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/this-revolutionary-new-observatory-will-locate-threatening-asteroids-and-millions-of-galaxies-180984514/ |access-date=March 24, 2025 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}} </ref><ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226">{{cite journal |last=Domonoske |first=Camila |date=December 26, 2016 |title=Vera Rubin, Who Confirmed Existence Of Dark Matter, Dies At 88 |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2016/12/26/507022497/vera-rubin-who-confirmed-existence-of-dark-matter-dies-at-88 |journal=[[NPR News]] |access-date=December 27, 2016}}</ref> Her legacy is described by ''[[The New York Times]]'' as "ushering in a [[Nicolaus Copernicus|Copernican]]-scale change" in [[Cosmology|cosmological theory]].<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /> Prominent theoretical physicist [[Lisa Randall]] and others have argued that Rubin was neglected for the Nobel Prize.<ref name="Randall-2017">{{Cite web |last=Randall |first=Lisa |date=January 4, 2017 |title=Why Vera Rubin Deserved a Nobel |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1855631918 |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=The New York Times |id={{ProQuest|1855631918}} |language=en}}</ref><ref name="scientificinquirer-2023">{{Cite web |last=scientificinquirer |date=January 17, 2023 |title=REBEL, REBEL: Vera Rubin was overlooked by the Nobel Committee but revered by the rest of us |url=https://scientificinquirer.com/2023/01/17/rebel-rebel-vera-rubin-overlooked-by-the-nobel-committee-but-revered-by-the-rest-of-us/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=scientificinquirer.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Feltman-2016">{{Cite web |last=Feltman |first=Rachel |date=December 27, 2016 |title=In memory of Vera Rubin, the woman the Nobel Prize forgot |url=https://www.popsci.com/in-memory-vera-rubin-woman-nobel-prize-forgot/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=Popular Science |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Gamillo-2023">{{Cite web |last=Gamillo |first=Elizabeth |date=December 25, 2023 |title=Vera Rubin: Biography, history of the trailblazing astronomer |url=https://www.astronomy.com/science/vera-rubin-found-a-lifetime-of-wonder-in-the-dark-skies/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=Astronomy |language=en-US}}</ref>

Rubin spent her life advocating for women in science, and mentored aspiring female astronomers.<ref name="The Observatory-1997">{{cite journal|date=June 1997|title=1996 November 8 meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society|journal=[[The Observatory (journal)|The Observatory]]|volume=117|pages=129–135|bibcode=1997Obs...117..129.}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Vera Cooper was born on July 23, 1928, in [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania. She was the younger of two sisters born to a [[Jewish]] family with roots in Eastern Europe.  Her father, Pesach Kobchefski, immigrated with his mother and three siblings to [[Gloversville, New York]], reuniting with his father who had immigrated a year or two earlier. Pesach soon [[anglicized]] his name to Pete Cooper, and as an adult studied [[electrical engineering]] and worked at [[Bell Telephone Company|Bell Telephone]]. He married Rose Applebaum, a second generation American born to a mother who had immigrated from [[Bessarabia]] (in present-day [[Moldova]] and [[Ukraine]]) to Philadelphia. They met at Bell, where Rose worked until they married.<ref name="Rubin-2001">{{cite journal |last=C. Rubin |first=Vera |author-link=Vera Rubin |date=September 2011 |title=An Interesting Voyage |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-astro-081710-102545 |journal=[[Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics]] |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=1–28 |doi=10.1146/annurev-astro-081710-102545 |bibcode=2011ARA&A..49....1R |access-date=May 27, 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1938 the family moved to Washington, D.C.,<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /> where ten-year-old Vera developed an interest in astronomy while watching the stars from her window.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="Bartusiak">{{Cite book | last=Bartusiak | first=Marcia | title=Through a Universe Darkly: A Cosmic Tale of Ancient Ethers, Dark Matter, and the Fate of the Universe | location=Toronto, Ontario, Canada | publisher=HarperCollins Canada | year=1993 | isbn=978-0060183103 | pages=needed | url=https://archive.org/details/throughuniversed00bart | access-date=December 29, 2016 }}</ref><ref name="jwa">{{cite book |last=Larsen |first=Kristine |title=Jewish Women: A comprehensive historical encyclopedia |date=March 2009 |publisher=[[Jewish Women's Archive]] |location=Brookline, MA |chapter=Vera Cooper Rubin |access-date=December 30, 2016 |chapter-url=https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/rubin-vera-cooper}}</ref> "Even then I was more interested in the question than in the answer," she remembered. "I decided at an early age that we inhabit a very curious world."<ref>{{cite web|title=The Doyenne of Dark Matter|url= https://www.theattic.space/home-page-blogs/2019/8/2/the-doyenne-of-dark-matter?rq=Vera%20rubin |website=The Attic| date=August 2, 2019 |access-date=November 5, 2019}}</ref> She built a crude [[telescope]] out of cardboard with her father, and began to observe and track [[Meteoroid|meteors]].<ref name="Irion">{{cite journal |last=Irion |first=Robert |date=February 8, 2002 |title=The bright face behind the dark sides of galaxies |journal=Science |volume=295 |issue=5557 |pages=960–961 |doi=10.1126/science.295.5557.960 |pmid=11834801 |s2cid=41891881}}</ref><ref name="Schudel-2016">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/vera-rubin-astronomer-who-verified-existence-of-dark-matter-dies-at-88/2016/12/26/545e617c-cb9d-11e6-a747-d03044780a02_story.html|title=Vera Rubin, astronomer who proved existence of dark matter, dies at 88|last=Schudel|first=Matt|date=December 26, 2016|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|access-date=July 7, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Scoles161004" /> She attended public school at [[Coolidge Senior High School (Washington, D.C.)|Coolidge Senior High School]], graduating in 1944.<ref name="Schudel-2016" />

Ignoring advice she had received from a high school science teacher to avoid a scientific career and become an artist,<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="Irion" /> the young aspiring astronomer chose instead to pursue her undergraduate education at [[Vassar College]]. Vassar, then an all-women's school, was famous for its association with the pioneering 19th century astronomer [[Maria Mitchell]], discoverer of Comet 1847 VI (modern designation C/1847 T1) and a professor at Vassar from the time of the founding of its [[Vassar College Observatory|observatory]] in 1865.<ref name=OverbyeNYT161227/>

At [[Vassar College]], Rubin was a member of the honors society [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Vera Cooper Rubin: Shedding light on dark matter |website=Innovators |publisher=Vassar College |url=https://innovators.vassar.edu/innovator.html?id=68 |access-date=March 8, 2018 |archive-date=March 6, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306234818/https://innovators.vassar.edu/innovator.html?id=68 |url-status=dead }}</ref> She earned her bachelor's degree in astronomy in 1948.<ref name="Irion" /> Despite Vassar's historic reputation for groundbreaking science in the field, Rubin was the only graduate in astronomy that year.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" />

=== Graduate studies ===
Rubin attempted to enroll in the astronomy program at [[Princeton University|Princeton]], but was barred due to her gender (Princeton would retain the policy of gender discrimination against women in its astronomy department until 1975<ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" />).<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="The Observatory-1997" />  She was accepted to Harvard's program, but declined the offer on the basis that she was getting married, and her future husband, a graduate student in physics, was based at [[Cornell University]].<ref name="Popova-2016">{{Cite web |last=Popova |first=Maria |date=April 18, 2016 |title=Pioneering Astronomer Vera Rubin on Women in Science, Dark Matter, and Our Never-Ending Quest to Know the Universe |url=https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/18/vera-rubin-interview-women-in-science/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=The Marginalian |language=en-US}}</ref>

Cornell was not known during this period for the excellence of its astronomy department, composed as it was of only four members. It did, however, boast an excellent physics faculty, and much of the coursework for Rubin's degree was taught within this department. Noted physicist [[Philip Morrison]] and future [[List of Nobel laureates|Nobelists]] [[Hans Bethe]] and [[Richard Feynman]] worked with Rubin during this period.<ref name="Scoles161004" /><ref name="Mitton-2021">{{Cite book |last1=Mitton |first1=Jacqueline |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HzQXEAAAQBAJ&q=Joshus |title=Vera Rubin: A Life |last2=Mitton |first2=Simon |year=2021 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-91919-8 |page=10 |language=en}}</ref>

At Cornell, she worked with astronomer Martha Carpenter on galactic dynamics and studied the motions of galaxies. From this work, Rubin made one of the first observations of deviations from [[Hubble's law|Hubble flow]].<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="Irion" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Vera Florence Cooper Rubin |website=The Bruce Medalists |publisher=[[Sonoma State University]] |url=http://www.phys-astro.sonoma.edu/BruceMedalists/Rubin/Rubin.html |access-date=July 6, 2017 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117023608/http://www.phys-astro.sonoma.edu/BruceMedalists/Rubin/Rubin.html |archive-date=January 17, 2018}}</ref> Though her conclusions – that there was an orbital motion of galaxies around a particular pole – were later disproven, the idea that galaxies were moving held true and sparked further research.<ref name="Irion" /> Additionally, Rubin's research provided early evidence of the [[Supergalactic coordinate system|supergalactic plane]].

This information and the data she compiled were controversial for their day. Against her advisors' hesitations, she gained permission to present at the annual meeting of [[American Astronomical Society]]. Not only was her material in a form that left it open to speculation that it was premature and incompletely supported, she had given birth to her first child three weeks previously and was not a member of the society.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yeager |first=Ashley Jean |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sHOdEAAAQBAJ&q=Vera+Rubin:+A+Life |title=Bright Galaxies, Dark Matter, and Beyond: The Life of Astronomer Vera Rubin |year=2023 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-54723-9 |page=53 |language=en}}</ref> These circumstances did not go unnoticed. Her presentation to the AAS in December 1950 received front page headlines ("Young Mother Has Own Theory of Universe", read the lede, disseminated from an article in the Washington Post<ref>{{Cite web |last=Blakesee |first=Howard |date=December 30, 1950 |title=Young Mother Has Own Theory of Universe |url=https://wikipedialibrary.wmflabs.org/?next_url=/ezproxy/r/ezp.2aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2Nlc3MubmV3c3BhcGVyYXJjaGl2ZS5jb20vdXMvbmV3LXlvcmsvY2FuYW5kYWlndWEvY2FuYW5kYWlndWEtZGFpbHktbWVzc2VuZ2VyLzE5NTAvMTItMzAvcGFnZS0x |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=Canandaigua Daily Messenger Newspaper Archives |page=1 |language=en}}</ref>). The talk received – to Rubin's personal recollection – universally negative feedback and the paper was not published.<ref name="Scoles161004" />

She completed her work at Cornell with the award of her 1951 master's degree.<ref name="Schudel-2016" />

Rubin studied next at [[Georgetown University]], where she earned her Ph.D. in 1954 (under [[George Gamow]], who was at nearby George Washington University),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vera Rubin and Dark Matter |url=https://www.amnh.org/learn-teach/curriculum-collections/cosmic-horizons-book/vera-rubin-dark-matter |website=American Museum of Natural History |series=Cosmic Horizons Curriculum Collection}}</ref> although much of her classwork was completed with Georgetownian [[Francis J. Heyden|Francis Heyden]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Vera Cooper Rubin |series=Women in Aviation and Space History |website=[[Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum]] |url=https://airandspace.si.edu/explore-and-learn/topics/women-in-aviation/rubin.cfm |access-date=July 7, 2017}}</ref> Her dissertation, completed in 1954, concluded that galaxies clumped together, rather than being randomly distributed through the universe, a controversial idea not pursued by others for two decades.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="Irion" /><ref name="CWP">{{cite book |last1 = Johnson |first1 = Ben |last2 = Tsai |first2 = Meigy |year = 2001 |editor1=Turner, Jean |editor2=Byers, Nina |editor2-link=Nina Byers |chapter = Vera Cooper Rubin |title = Contributions of 20th&nbsp;Century Women to Physics (CWP) |location = Los Angeles, CA |publisher = [[University of California]] |chapter-url = http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Rubin,_Vera_Cooper@931234567.html |url-status = dead |access-date = December 29, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130424105951/http://www.physics.ucla.edu/~cwp/Phase2/Rubin%2C_Vera_Cooper%40931234567.html |archive-date = April 24, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Popova-2016" />

== Career ==
[[File:Vera Rubin measuring spectra (cropped).jpg|thumb|Rubin in 1972, measuring spectra at the Carnegie Institution in Washington, D.C.]]
For the next decade, Rubin held various short-term academic positions in the greater DC area. She served for a year as an instructor of Mathematics and Physics at [[Montgomery College]], Maryland. Then from 1955 to 1965 she worked at Georgetown University as a research associate astronomer, lecturer (1959–1962), and finally, assistant professor of astronomy (1962–1965).<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="CWP"/>

In the latter position, from 1963, Rubin began a year-long collaboration with [[Geoffrey Burbidge|Geoffrey]] and [[Margaret Burbidge]], during which she made her first observations of the rotation of galaxies while using the [[McDonald Observatory]]'s 82-inch telescope.<ref name="Irion" />

She joined the [[Carnegie Institution of Washington]] (later called Carnegie Institution of Science) in 1965 as a staff member in the Department of [[Earth's magnetic field|Terrestrial Magnetism]].<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="CWP" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dtm.ciw.edu/users/rubin/%7D%7D|title=Vera C. Rubin|website=Carnegie Institution: Department of Terrestrial Magnetism|access-date=December 29, 2016}}</ref> There she met her long-time collaborator, instrument-maker [[Kent Ford (astronomer)|Kent Ford]].<ref name="Irion" />

During her work at the Carnegie Institution, Rubin applied to become the first female astronomer permitted to observe at the [[Palomar Observatory]] in 1965.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.popsci.com/in-memory-vera-rubin-woman-nobel-prize-forgot|title=In memory of Vera Rubin, the woman the Nobel Prize forgot|last=Feltman|first=Rachel|date=December 27, 2016|work=Popular Science|access-date=October 23, 2017}}</ref><ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="GruberFoundation-2016">{{cite web |title=Vera Rubin |url=http://gruber.yale.edu/cosmology/vera-rubin |access-date=December 26, 2016 |website=The Gruber Foundation}}</ref>

An initiating faculty member of the [[Vatican Observatory]] Summer School (1986), Rubin continued this relationship through subsequent decades, providing dedication remarks for the opening of the [[Vatican Advanced Technology Telescope|VATT]], the Vatican's telescope on Mount Graham.<ref name="Consolmagno-2016" />

Rubin retired from the Carnegie Institute in 2014 as Senior Fellow of Astronomy in the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism.<ref name="National Space Grant Foundation-2010">{{Cite web |date=2010 |title=Dr. Vera Rubin  |url=https://spacegrant.org/programs/service-award/rubin/ |access-date=March 26, 2025 |website=National Space Grant Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Carnegie Science">{{Cite web |title=Vera C. Rubin Photograph Collection, circa 1942–2012 |url=https://archivesspace.carnegiescience.edu/repositories/3/resources/26 |access-date=March 25, 2025 |website=Carnegie Science}}</ref> [[File:Vera Rubin using Kitt Peak National Observatory's 36-inch telescope.jpg|thumb|Rubin in the 1970s using [[Kitt Peak National Observatory]]'s 36-inch telescope with Kent Ford's image tube spectrograph attached|alt=Photo of Rubin adjusting part of a large telescope]]

== Research ==
At the Carnegie Institution, Rubin began work related to her controversial thesis regarding galaxy clusters in tandem with Kent Ford,<ref name="CWP" /> making hundreds of observations using Ford's image-tube [[spectrograph]].<ref name="Carnegie-2013">{{Cite web|url=https://dtm.carnegiescience.edu/news/kent-ford-vera-rubins-image-tube-spectrograph-named-smithsonians-101-objects-made-america|title=Kent Ford & Vera Rubin's Image Tube Spectrograph named in Smithsonian's '101 Objects that Made America'|website=DTM (Carnegie Science)|date=November 26, 2013 |access-date=October 23, 2017}}</ref> This [[image intensifier]] allowed resolving the spectra of astronomical objects that were previously too dim for spectral analysis.<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="Carnegie-2013" /> A decade of observations coalesced in the shared discovery of the Rubin-Ford effect, with publication first appearing in 1976.

=== Rubin–Ford effect ===
{{Main|Rubin–Ford effect}}

The Rubin–Ford effect, an apparent [[anisotropy]] in the [[expansion of the Universe]] on the scale of 100 million light years, was discovered through studies of [[spiral galaxies]], particularly the [[Andromeda Galaxy]], chosen for its brightness and proximity to Earth.<ref name="Scoles161004" /><ref name="OxfordRef">{{cite book | editor = Ridpath, Ian | year = 2016 | orig-year = 2012
 | title = A Dictionary of Astronomy | edition = 2nd, revised | chapter = Rubin–Ford Effect | page = 406 | location = Oxford, UK | publisher = Oxford University Press | isbn = 9780199609055 }} See also the [http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100432262 publishers online entry].</ref> The idea of [[peculiar motion]] on this scale in the universe was a highly controversial proposition. It was dismissed by leading astronomers but ultimately shown to be valid.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="Scoles161004">{{cite news|url=http://www.astronomy.com/news/2016/10/vera-rubin
 |title=How Vera Rubin Discovered Dark Matter|last=Scoles|first=Sarah|date=October 4, 2016
|work=Astronomy|access-date=December 26, 2016}}</ref> The effect is now known as [[Stellar_kinematics#Stellar_streams| large scale streaming]].<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" />

=== Galactic motion ===
Rubin and Kent also briefly studied [[quasar]]s, which had been discovered in the early 1960s and were a popular topic of research.<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="Scoles161004" /> Wishing to avoid controversial areas of astronomy, including quasars and galactic motion, Rubin began to study the rotation and outer reaches of galaxies, an interest sparked by her collaboration with the Burbidges.<ref name="Irion" />

==== Rotational curves ====
She investigated the rotation curves of spiral galaxies, again beginning with Andromeda, by looking at their outermost material. She observed flat rotation curves: the outermost components of the galaxy were moving as quickly as those close to the center.<ref name="Bahcall-2017a">{{Cite journal|last=Bahcall|first=Neta A.|date=February 28, 2017|title=Vera C. Rubin: Pioneering American astronomer (1928–2016)|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=114|issue=9|pages=2099–2100|doi=10.1073/pnas.1701066114|issn=0027-8424|pmc=5338491|pmid=28167783|bibcode=2017PNAS..114.2099B |doi-access=free}}</ref>  She further uncovered the discrepancy between the predicted [[angular motion]] of galaxies based on the visible light and the observed motion.<ref name="Tucker1988">{{cite book|title=The Dark Matter|url=https://archive.org/details/darkmattercontem00tuck|url-access=registration|last2=Tucker|first2=Karen|date=1988|publisher=William Morrow|isbn=9780688103880|last1=Tucker|first1=Wallace}}</ref> Her research showed that spiral galaxies rotate quickly enough that they should fly apart, if the gravity of their constituent stars was all that was holding them together; because they stay intact, a large amount of unseen mass must be holding them together, a conundrum that became known as the galaxy rotation problem.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="Bahcall-2017a" />

Rubin's results came to be cited as evidence that spiral galaxies were surrounded by [[dark matter halo]]es.<ref name="RubinDarkMatter2006">{{Cite journal |last=Rubin |first=Vera |date=December 1, 2006 |title=Seeing dark matter in the Andromeda galaxy |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/59/12/8/387114/Seeing-dark-matter-in-the-Andromeda-galaxy |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=59 |issue=12 |pages=8–9 |doi=10.1063/1.2435662 |bibcode=2006PhT....59l...8R |issn=0031-9228 |quote=Our study was influential in the later conclusion that most of the matter in the universe is dark.}}</ref><ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref name="Irion" />
Rubin's calculations showed that galaxies must contain at least five to ten times more mass than can be observed directly based on the light emitted by ordinary matter.<ref name="Carnegie-2016">{{Cite web|url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/vera-rubin-who-confirmed-%E2%80%9Cdark-matter%E2%80%9D-dies|title=Vera Rubin Who Confirmed 'Dark Matter' Dies|date=December 26, 2016|website=Carnegie Science|access-date=July 7, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Randall2015">{{cite book |last=Randall |first= Lisa|author-link=Lisa Randall|date=2015 |title=Dark Matter and the Dinosaurs |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=9780062328502 }}</ref> Rubin's results were confirmed over subsequent decades,<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /> and became the first persuasive results supporting the theory of dark matter, initially proposed by [[Fritz Zwicky]] in the 1930s.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="Scoles161004" /><ref name="Peebles1993">{{cite book|title=Principles of Physical Cosmology|last=Peebles|first=P.J.E.|date=1993|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0691019338|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/principlesofphys00pjep}}</ref> This data was confirmed by radio astronomers, the discovery of the [[cosmic microwave background]], and images of [[gravitational lens]]ing.<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="Scoles161004" /> However, Rubin did not rule out<ref name=RubinHistoyr>{{Cite book |last=Rubin |first=Vera C. |title=The Dark Universe: Matter, Energy and Gravity |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-139-44980-9 |editor-last=Livio |editor-first=M. |series=Space Telescope Science Institute Symposium Series |pages=1–13 |chapter=A brief history of dark matter |quote=A few brave, smart cosmologists work to modify Newton's laws to account for the observations. |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cQybKATqbmMC&pg=PA1}}</ref> alternative models to dark matter also inspired by her measurements.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /> She and her research were discussed in the 1991 PBS series, ''The Astronomers''.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Astronomers Complete PBS Series on Astronomy | website=Internet Archive | date=March 25, 2023 | url=https://archive.org/details/the-astronomers-1991 | access-date=January 7, 2024}}</ref>

==== Counter-rotation ====
Another area of interest for Rubin was the phenomenon of counter-rotation in galaxies. Her discovery that some gas and stars moved in the opposite direction to the rotation of the rest of the galaxy challenged the prevailing theory that all of the material in a galaxy moved in the same direction, and provided the first evidence for [[galaxy merger]]s and the process by which galaxies initially formed.<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" />

== Activism for women in astronomy ==
[[File:Several women scientists who changed astronomy.tif|thumb|Famous astronomers: Vera Rubin (2nd from left), [[Wendy Freedman]] (3rd), [[Sandra Faber]] (4th), [[Nancy Roman]] (6th). 1988]]

During her work at the Carnegie Institution, Rubin applied to observe at the [[Palomar Observatory]] in 1965, despite the fact that the building did not have facilities for women. Reluctantly granted access, she was informed "your time on the observatory is limited, because we don't have a women's bathroom,"<ref name="Isaacs" /> a common period ruse to avoid allowing women access to these stations (Margaret Burbridge faced similar discrimination at Carnegie a decade previous, when she gained access to the telescope at the [[Mount Wilson Observatory]] via the pretense that husband Geoffrey was the telescope operator). According to Carnegie president [[Eric Isaacs]], Rubin "solved the problem pretty simply by cutting out a little paper skirt and taping it to the stick figure image of a man which was on the men's room door. And she turned around and said, 'now you have a ladies' room' and then she got to work."<ref name="Isaacs">{{Cite web |last=Isaacs |first=Eric |date= |title=Remembering Vera Rubin |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/remembering-vera-rubin |access-date=March 25, 2025 |website=carnegiescience.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Throughout her graduate studies, Rubin encountered discouraging sexism; in one incident she was not allowed to meet with her advisor in his office, because women were not allowed in that area of Georgetown, a Catholic university.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="Irion" /> Motivated by her own battles to gain credibility in a field dominated by male astronomers, Rubin encouraged girls interested in investigating the universe to pursue their dreams. She was described by [[Sandra Faber]] and [[Neta Bahcall]] as one of the astronomers who paved the way for other women in the field, as a "guiding light" for those who wished to have families and careers in astronomy. [[Rebecca Oppenheimer]] also recalled Rubin's mentorship as important to her early career.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="Carnegie-2016" /><ref name="Drake-2016">{{Cite journal |last=Drake |first=Nadia |author-link=Nadia Drake |date=December 27, 2016 |title=Vera Rubin, Pioneering Astronomer, Dies at 88 |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/12/vera-rubin-dark-matter-galaxy-rotation-nobel-science |url-status=dead |journal=National Geographic |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228143112/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/12/vera-rubin-dark-matter-galaxy-rotation-nobel-science/ |archive-date=December 28, 2016 |access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Bahcall-2017a" /><ref name="Bahcall-2017b" />

When Rubin was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (NAS) in 1981, she became only the second woman astronomer in its ranks (after her colleague [[Margaret Burbidge]]).<ref name="Irion" /> She, alongside Burbidge, advocated for more women to be elected to the NAS, selected for review panels, and represented in academic searches. She said that despite her own election to the NAS, she continued to be dissatisfied with the low number of women who were elected each year, and she further said it was "the saddest part of [her] life".<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="Scoles161004" /><ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" />

Throughout her life, Rubin faced discouraging comments on her choice of study but persevered, as she was supported by family and colleagues.<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" /> In addition to encouraging women in astronomy, she was a force for greater recognition of [[women in the sciences]] and for [[scientific literacy]].<ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" /><ref name="Drake-2016" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grant |first=Andrew |date=December 27, 2016 |title=Vera Rubin in the pages of Physics Today |journal=Physics Today |issue=12 |article-number=12140 |bibcode=2016PhT..2016l2140G |doi=10.1063/pt.5.9080}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
[[File:Vera Rubin AIP.jpg|thumb|Vera Rubin]]
Rubin married in 1948, when her husband, [[Robert Joshua Rubin]], was a graduate student at Cornell University, and she herself had recently graduated from Vassar.<ref name="VOX-20210817" /><ref name="Irion" /> She was 23 years old and pregnant with her second child when she began her doctoral studies.<ref name="OverbyeNYT161227" /><ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" />

By 1963, Rubin, working and with four children, was described as the sole member of Vassar's class of 1948 as having "come near to filling the Utopian aim of being a full-time professional in her field without, for the most part, putting her children into someone else's hands".<ref name="Rifkin-1963">{{Cite journal |last=Rifkin |first=Natalie Stone |date=June 1, 1963 |title=Trapped or Challenged? A Report on the Class of 1948 |url=https://newspaperarchives.vassar.edu/?a=d&d=vq19630601-01.2.11&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------- |journal=Poughkeepsie Vassar Alumnae Quarterly Newspaper Archives |pages=21–25}}</ref> Rubin ascribed this characterization to the "unique part time full time" nature of her then position at Georgetown University.<ref name="Rifkin-1963" /> Because she had young children, she did much of her work from home.<ref name="Schudel-2016" />

All four of their children earned PhDs in the [[natural science]]s or mathematics: David (born 1950), is a geologist with the [[U.S. Geological Survey]]; [[Judith Young (astronomer)|Judith Young]] (1952–2014), was an astronomer at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]]; [[Karl Rubin|Karl]] (born 1956), is a mathematician at the [[University of California, Irvine]]; and Allan (born 1960), is a geologist at Princeton University.<ref name="jwa" /><ref name="Irion" /><ref name="Bahcall-2017b">{{Cite journal |last=Bahcall |first=Neta A. |date=February 2, 2017 |title=Vera Rubin (1928–2016) |journal=Nature |volume=542 |issue=7639 |pages=32 |bibcode=2017Natur.542...32B |doi=10.1038/542032a |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=28150763 |s2cid=4464509}}</ref> Rubin's children recalled later in life that their mother made a life of science appear desirable and fun, which inspired them to become scientists themselves.<ref name="Irion" />

Rubin was [[Jewish]], and she said she saw no conflict between [[science and religion]]. In an interview, she said: "In my own life, my science and my religion are separate. I'm Jewish, and so religion to me is a kind of moral code and a kind of history. I try to do my science in a moral way, and, I believe that, ideally, science should be looked upon as something that helps us understand our role in the universe."<ref>{{cite web |last=Meyer |first=Gabriel |date=December 1–7, 1996 |title=Pontifical Science Academy Banks on Stellar Cast |url=http://www.ewtn.com/library/ISSUES/STELLAR.TXT |access-date=October 19, 2010 |website=Eternal Word Television Network}}</ref>

Rubin's older sister, Ruth Cooper Burg, was an attorney who later worked as an [[administrative law judge]] in the [[United States Department of Defense]].<ref name="Bartusiak" />

In the early 2000s, Vera Rubin was still actively engaged in scientific work, and in 2013 articles with her participation were still being published.<ref>[https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/search/fq=%7B!type%3Daqp%20v%3D%24fq_database%7D&fq_database=(database%3Aastronomy%20OR%20database%3Aphysics)&q=%20author%3A%22Rubin%2C%20Vera%20C.%22&sort=date%20desc%2C%20bibcode%20desc&p_=0 Articles by Vera Rubin] NASA ADS</ref> In 2008, [[Robert Joshua Rubin]], Vera Rubin's husband, with whom she had been married for about 60 years, died.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/02/04/AR2008020403043.html|title=Robert J. Rubin, 81; Scientist Whose Work Combined Disciplines|last=Sullivan|first=Patricia|date=February 5, 2008|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref>

Rubin died of natural causes at age 88 on the night of December 25, 2016.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 26, 2016 |title=Vera Rubin, pioneering astronomer, dies at 88 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-38440291 |access-date=March 26, 2025 |publisher=[[BBC News]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> She had [[dementia]] and was living in an assisted living facility.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thejc.com/news/world/vera-rubin-the-astronomer-who-identified-dark-matter-dies-aged-88-wrjuze9w|title=Vera Rubin, the astronomer who identified dark matter, dies aged 88 Pioneering American scientist should have won the Nobel Prize for her revolutionary work, says colleague|work=The Jewish Chronicle|date=December 28, 2016|first=Lianne|last=Kolirin|accessdate=March 26, 2025}}</ref> Rubin was memorialized by her colleagues at the Carnegie Institution, where she performed the bulk of her work and research, as a national treasure.<ref name="DomonoskeNPR161226" /><ref name="Carnegie-2016" />

== Legacy ==

===Nobel Prize controversy===
Rubin is "widely thought to have been snubbed for the Nobel Prize".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harper |first=Arthur |title=LibGuides: Women in STEM: Vera Rubin |url=https://guides.library.duq.edu/c.php?g=972534&p=7029805 |access-date=March 24, 2025 |website=guides.library.duq.edu |language=en}}</ref> In the decade following her death, there has been significant ongoing disagreement as to why Rubin's work was not recognized with a Nobel Prize. Some assume it was "because of her gender,"<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 6, 2020 |title=Vera Rubin |url=https://www.mothersinscience.com/trailblazers/vera-rubin |access-date=March 24, 2025 |website=Mothers in Science |language=en-US}}</ref> while physicists such as [[Lisa Randall]] and [[Emily Levesque]] have argued that it was an oversight.<ref name="Scoles161004" /><ref name="Randall-2017">{{Cite web |last=Randall |first=Lisa |date=January 4, 2017 |title=Why Vera Rubin Deserved a Nobel |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1855631918 |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=The New York Times |id={{ProQuest|1855631918}} |language=en}}</ref>  Others have argued that it was a "glaring omission".<ref name="Gamillo-2023">{{Cite web |last=Gamillo |first=Elizabeth |date=December 25, 2023 |title=Vera Rubin: Biography, history of the trailblazing astronomer |url=https://www.astronomy.com/science/vera-rubin-found-a-lifetime-of-wonder-in-the-dark-skies/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=Astronomy |language=en-US}}</ref> Popularly written articles like ''[[Forbes]]''<nowiki/>' "Who Really Discovered Dark Matter: [[Fritz Zwicky]] Or Vera Rubin?"<ref name="Siegel-2010">{{Cite web |last=Siegel |first=Ethan |date=August 21, 2010 |title=Who Really Discovered Dark Matter: Fritz Zwicky Or Vera Rubin? |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2021/08/24/who-really-discovered-dark-matter-fritz-zwicky-or-vera-rubin/ |access-date=March 26, 2025 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> both characterize Rubin's failure to be awarded a Nobel Prize as an egregious snub<ref name="Siegel-2010" /> and equivocate regarding the specific science on which this honor would have been conferred.

Discussion of the issue continues, as posthumous honors and recognition (see below) have proliferated, and Rubin's name is regularly mentioned in articles listing the 20th century women who missed out on Nobel Prizes.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Paul |first=Anna |date=October 7, 2018 |title=Five women who missed out on the Nobel prize |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/oct/07/five-women-the-nobel-prize-missed |access-date=March 25, 2025 |work=The Observer |language=en-GB |issn=0029-7712}}</ref><ref name="Feltman-2016">{{Cite web |last=Feltman |first=Rachel |date=December 27, 2016 |title=In memory of Vera Rubin, the woman the Nobel Prize forgot |url=https://www.popsci.com/in-memory-vera-rubin-woman-nobel-prize-forgot/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=Popular Science |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Randall-2017" /><ref name="NYT-20200111" /><ref name="scientificinquirer-2023">{{Cite web |last=scientificinquirer |date=January 17, 2023 |title=REBEL, REBEL: Vera Rubin was overlooked by the Nobel Committee but revered by the rest of us |url=https://scientificinquirer.com/2023/01/17/rebel-rebel-vera-rubin-overlooked-by-the-nobel-committee-but-revered-by-the-rest-of-us/ |access-date=March 22, 2025 |website=scientificinquirer.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[File:Rubin Observatory and Its Target.jpg|270x270px|thumb|The [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]] and the [[Milky Way]]]]

=== Vera C. Rubin Observatory ===
[[File:Some Assembly Required.jpg|thumb|Telescope Mount Assembly of the 8.4-meter Simonyi Survey Telescope at [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]], under construction atop Cerro Pachón in Chile|270x270px]]

On December 20, 2019, the [[Large Synoptic Survey Telescope]] was renamed the [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]] in recognition of Rubin's contributions to the study of dark matter and her outspoken advocacy for the equal treatment and representation of women in science.<ref name="NYT-20200111">{{cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |author-link=Dennis Overbye |date=January 11, 2020 |title=Vera Rubin Gets a Telescope of Her Own – The astronomer missed her Nobel Prize. But she now has a whole new observatory to her name. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/11/science/vera-rubin-telescope-astronomy.html |access-date=January 11, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Johnson |first=Eddie Bernice |date=December 20, 2019 |title=H.R. 3196 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Vera C. Rubin Observatory Designation Act |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/3196 |access-date=December 27, 2019 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=January 7, 2020 |title=NSF-supported observatory renamed for astronomer Vera C. Rubin |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=299739 |access-date=January 8, 2020 |website=www.nsf.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Koren |first=Marina |date=January 9, 2020 |title=An Influential Female Astronomer Is Getting Her Due |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2020/01/vera-rubin-observatory/604624/ |access-date=January 11, 2020 |website=The Atlantic |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="nsf">{{cite web |date=2016 |title=National Medal of Science 50th Anniversary: Vera Rubin (1928– ) |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/rubin.jsp |access-date=December 26, 2016 |publisher=National Science Foundation (NSF) |location=Arlington, Virginia, US}}</ref> The observatory is located on a mountain in [[Cerro Pachón]], [[Chile]] and observations will focus on the study of dark matter and [[dark energy]]. As of April 2025, the telescope had begun operation and was producing images and volumes of new data.<ref>"This Powerful Telescope Quickly Found 2,100 New Asteroids," by Kenneth Chang, ''New York Times'', June 23, 2025</ref>

=== Additional recognition ===
* In 2002, ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized Rubin as one of the 50 most important women in science.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite news |last1=Svitil |first1=Kathy |date=November 13, 2002 |title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science |url=http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/ |access-date=May 1, 2019 |publisher=Discover}}</ref>
* On November 6, 2020, a satellite named after her ([[ÑuSat|ÑuSat 18]] or "Vera", COSPAR 2020-079K) was launched into space.
* An area on [[Mars]], Vera Rubin Ridge, is named after her, as well as the asteroid [[5726 Rubin]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kremer |first=Ken |date=October 19, 2017 |title=Sky Pointing Curiosity Captures Breathtaking Vista of Mount Sharp and Crater Rim, Climbs Vera Rubin Seeking Hydrated Martian Minerals |url=https://www.universetoday.com/136671/sky-pointing-curiosity-captures-breathtaking-vista-of-mount-sharp-and-crater-rim-climbs-vera-rubin-seeking-hydrated-minerals/ |access-date=October 23, 2017 |work=Universe Today}}</ref>
* Rubin is honored on a 2025 [[U.S. quarter]] as part of the final year of the [[American Women quarters]] program.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 17, 2023 |title=United States Mint Announces 2025 American Women Quarters™ Program Coins |url=https://www.usmint.gov/news/press-releases/united-states-mint-announces-2025-american-women-quarters-program-coins/ |access-date=October 17, 2023 |website=United States Mint |archive-date=December 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231201102308/https://www.usmint.gov/news/press-releases/united-states-mint-announces-2025-american-women-quarters-program-coins |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* In 2024, [[Nvidia]] announced that their next generation of data center accelerators would be named after her, with the [[Central processing unit|CPU]] named Vera and [[Graphics processing unit|GPU]] named [[Rubin (microarchitecture)|Rubin]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hagedoorn |first=Hilbert |date=June 2, 2024 |title=NVIDIA Confirms Next-Generation Architecture is based on (Vera) Rubin GPU |url=https://www.guru3d.com/story/nvidia-confirms-nextgeneration-architecture-is-based-on-vera-rubin-gpu/ |access-date=June 2, 2024 |website=www.guru3d.com |language=en}}</ref>
* The Carnegie Institution has created a postdoctoral research fund in Rubin's honor.<ref name="Carnegie-2016" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=January 25, 2017 |title=Vera Rubin Fellowship |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/projects/vera-rubin-fellowship |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170718024340/https://carnegiescience.edu/projects/vera-rubin-fellowship |archive-date=July 18, 2017 |access-date=July 7, 2017 |website=Carnegie Science}}</ref>
* The [[Division on Dynamical Astronomy]] of the [[American Astronomical Society]] has named the [[Vera Rubin Early Career Prize]] in her honor. It seeks to recognize excellence in [[Celestial mechanics|dynamical astronomy]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 10, 2017 |title=DDA's New Early Career Prize Named for Vera Rubin |url=https://aas.org/posts/news/2017/01/ddas-new-early-career-prize-named-vera-rubin |access-date=July 7, 2017 |website=American Astronomical Society}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Vera Rubin Early Career Prize |url=https://dda.aas.org/awards/rubin |access-date=July 7, 2017 |website=Division on Dynamical Astronomy}}</ref>

=== Media ===
* The Verubin Nebula, which appears in season three of ''[[Star Trek: Discovery (season 3)|Star Trek: Discovery]]'', is named after Rubin.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=January 11, 2021|title=Tweet of Erin Macdonald, PhD.|url=https://twitter.com/drerinmac/status/1348740793092239363|access-date=|website=}}</ref>
* Rubin was featured in an animated segment of the 13th and final episode of ''[[Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey]]''.<ref>{{cite web |year=2013 |title=Vera Rubin's Influential Work on Dark Matter is Highlighted in Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey |url=https://dtm.carnegiescience.edu/news/vera-rubins-influential-work-dark-matter-highlighted-cosmos-spacetime-odyssey |access-date=December 26, 2016 |work=Department of Terrestrial Magnetism (DTM), Carnegie Institution of Washington}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
[[File:Design of U S quarter featuring Dr Vera C Rubin (rubin-2025-americanwomen-quarterscoin-verarubin).jpg|thumb|Rubin is honored on a 2025 edition of the [[American Women quarters]] series]]
Following her 1981 election as the second woman ever to the National Academy of Sciences,<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=March 1, 2021 |title=Vera Florence Cooper Rubin {{!}} Philadelphia Women's History Month All-Star |url=https://thephiladelphiacitizen.org/vera-rubin-biography/ |access-date=March 25, 2025 |website=The Philadelphia Citizen |language=en-US}}</ref> Rubin and her work received numerous accolades.{{Synthesis inline|date=June 2025}} 

Rubin's perspective on the history of the work on galaxy movements was presented in a review, "One Hundred Years of Rotating Galaxies," for the ''[[Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific]]'' in 2000. This was an adaptation of the lecture she gave in 1996 upon receiving the Gold Medal of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]], the second woman to be so honored, 168 years after [[Caroline Herschel]] received the Medal in 1828.<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref>{{cite journal |last=Rubin |first=Vera |year=2000 |title=One Hundred Years of Rotating Galaxies |url=https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Sept04/Rubin/paper.pdf |journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific |volume=112 |issue=June |pages=747–750 |bibcode=2000PASP..112..747R |doi=10.1086/316573 |s2cid=122927800 |access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref>
* [[National Space Grant College and Fellowship Program|National Space Grant]] Distinguished Service Award (2010)<ref name="National Space Grant Foundation-2010" />
* [[Adler Planetarium]] Lifetime Achievement Award (2009)<ref>{{cite web |title=Lifetime Achievement Award |url=http://www.panacheprivee.com/Web/BeSeen/AdlerPlanetarium09/Women_in_Space_Science_Awards.asp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131104211645/http://www.panacheprivee.com/Web/BeSeen/AdlerPlanetarium09/Women_in_Space_Science_Awards.asp |archive-date=November 4, 2013 |access-date=February 20, 2013}}</ref>
* [[Richtmyer Memorial Award]] (2008)<ref>{{cite web |title=News – Carnegie Institution for Science |url=http://carnegiescience.edu/news/carnegie_s_vera_rubin_receive_richtmyer_award |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120612104904/http://carnegiescience.edu/news/carnegie_s_vera_rubin_receive_richtmyer_award |archive-date=June 12, 2012 |access-date=December 29, 2016 |work=Carnegie Science}}</ref>
* [[James Craig Watson Medal]] of the National Academy of Sciences (2004)<ref>{{cite web |title=James Craig Watson Medal |url=http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/james-craig-watson-medal.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130723073436/http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/james-craig-watson-medal.html |archive-date=July 23, 2013 |access-date=February 20, 2013 |website=NAS}}</ref><ref name="Bahcall-2017a" />
* [[Bruce Medal|Catherine Wolfe Bruce Gold Medal]] of the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]] (2003)<ref>{{cite web |date=2003 |title=Vera Rubin Wins 2003 ASP Bruce Medal and Other ASP Award Winners |url=http://www.astrosociety.org/membership/awards/03winnerspr.html |access-date=December 26, 2016 |publisher=Astronomical Society of the Pacific (ASP) |location=San Francisco, California}}</ref>
* [[Gruber Prize in Cosmology|Gruber International Cosmology Prize]] (2002)<ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 Gruber Cosmology Prize |url=http://gruber.yale.edu/prize/2002-gruber-cosmology-prize |access-date=July 6, 2017 |website=The Gruber Foundation}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2002 Gruber Cosmology Prize Press Release |url=http://gruber.yale.edu/cosmology/press/2002-gruber-cosmology-prize-press-release |access-date=December 26, 2016 |publisher=The Gruber Foundation}}</ref>
* [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] (1996)<ref name="The Observatory-1997" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Winners of the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society |url=https://www.ras.org.uk/awards-and-grants/awards/268 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160630050255/http://www.ras.org.uk/awards-and-grants/awards/268/ |archive-date=June 30, 2016 |access-date=December 29, 2016 |work=Royal Astronomical Society}}</ref><ref name="CWP" /> (the first women to receive this honor since [[Caroline Herschel]], awarded the prize in 1828<ref name="Carnegie Science" />)
* [[Weizmann Women & Science Award]] (1996)<ref>{{cite web |title=Recipients |url=http://www.weizmann.ac.il/WomenInScience/weizmann-women-science-award/recipients |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822160408/http://www.weizmann.ac.il/WomenInScience/weizmann-women-science-award/recipients |archive-date=August 22, 2016 |access-date=December 31, 2016 |work=Weizmann Women & Science Award}}</ref>
* Member, [[Pontifical Academy of Sciences]] (appointed 1996)<ref name="Consolmagno-2016">{{Cite web |last1=Consolmagno |first1=Guy |last2=Corbally |first2=Chris |date=December 30, 2016 |title=Dr. Vera Rubin |url=https://www.vaticanobservatory.org/sacred-space-astronomy/dr-vera-rubin/ |access-date=March 25, 2025 |website=Vatican Observatory |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /><ref>{{cite web |date=March 27, 2012 |title=Women's History Month – Vera Rubin |url=http://www.13point7billion.org/2012/03/womens-history-month-vera-rubin.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161227055846/http://www.13point7billion.org/2012/03/womens-history-month-vera-rubin.html |archive-date=December 27, 2016 |access-date=December 26, 2016 |website=13.7 Billion Years}}</ref>
* Member, [[American Philosophical Society]] (elected 1995)<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Members' Directory Search |url=http://www.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170401175306/http://www.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search |archive-date=April 1, 2017 |access-date=December 26, 2016 |website=American Philosophical Society}}</ref>
* [[Henry Norris Russell Lectureship]], American Astronomical Society (1994)<ref>{{cite web |title=Henry Norris Russell Lectureship |url=http://aas.org/about/grants-and-prizes/henry-norris-russell-lectureship |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160119022215/http://aas.org/about/grants-and-prizes/henry-norris-russell-lectureship |archive-date=January 19, 2016 |access-date=December 26, 2016 |publisher=American Astronomical Society}}</ref>
* [[Dickson Prize for Science]] (1994)<ref>{{cite web |title=Dickson Prize |url=http://www.nndb.com/honors/045/000111709/ |access-date=December 26, 2016 |website=NNDB}}</ref>
* [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory#Jansky Prize|Jansky Lectureship]] before the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory]] (1994)<ref>{{cite web |title=Jansky Lecture Redirect |url=http://www.nrao.edu/jansky/janskyprize.shtml |access-date=December 26, 2016}}</ref>
* [[National Medal of Science]] (1993)<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /><ref name="nsf2">{{cite web |author=NSF Staff |date=2016 |title=National Medal of Science 50th Anniversary: Vera Rubin (1928– ) |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/rubin.jsp |access-date=December 26, 2016 |publisher=National Science Foundation (NSF) |location=Arlington, Virginia, US}}</ref>
* Member, [[National Academy of Sciences]] (elected 1981)<ref name="Irion" /><ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/vera-c-rubin-pt9pw2/|title=Vera Rubin|date=2016|publisher=National Academy of Sciences (NAS)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161227061125/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/51005.html|archive-date=December 27, 2016|url-status=live|access-date=December 26, 2016}}</ref>
In addition to this list, Rubin was granted [[honorary doctorates]] from [[Harvard University]],<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /> [[Yale University]],<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /> [[Smith College]],<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /> [[Grinnell College]],<ref name="GruberFoundation-2016" /> and [[Princeton University]] (2005).<ref name="Bahcall-2017b" />

== Quotations ==
"Don't let anyone keep you down for silly reasons such as who you are. And don't worry about prizes and fame. The real prize is finding something new out there."<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 20, 2025 |title=Remembering Vera: Vera Rubin In Memoriam, Discover More |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/remembering-vera |access-date=March 25, 2025 |website=Carnegie Science |language=en}}</ref>
